title: Jay Leno Explores the Roots of the Baja Beetle

body_markdown:
Of all the cars that would end up as the go-to base for kit cars and the half-stripped machines that came to be known as dune buggies, the Volkswagen Beetle is likely the least surprising. Its cheery, durable, and simple nature provides the exact attributes sought by people who enjoy building their own fun. Among those people is Porsche guru Rod Emory, who brought a pair of dune buggies with him on a recent trip to[Jay Leno’s Garage](https://youtu.be/lT8Moy30KAg?si=INOLn4ADlITUh1uz) .


Emory is from a gearhead family that has called Southern California home for over 50 years. Dune buggies and their culture were something the Emory family was on the leading edge of—Rod’s father and grandfather worked in shops in Newport Beach, California, as off-roading became ever more popular. They wheeled and dealed to get an early Beetle, but is wasn’t long before they cut it up and altered it into something tailored for carving big sand waves.


The kits to completely re-body the VW in the style of Bruce Meyers and the[Meyers Manx](https://driversfoundation.org/articles/first-manx-dune-buggy-at-the-henry-ford) existed but, while not expensive, were also not as cost-effective as leaving most of the body alone and replacing portions of it with fiberglass. The Emory family’s chopped-up creation is said to have inspired the first fiberglass hood and fender kits for VW Beetles. These kits only became more popular as the price for a used Beetle continued to drop over the years.

The beauty in a dune buggy is the lack of rigid requirements to make one, and the wide-open possibilities of putting it to use. Strip down a simple car, then go out and drive on the dunes or just go explore a few trails, as Jay and Rod did in the yellow Beetle that was built in tribute to the first dune buggy his family built so long ago. The original got rolled and destroyed, but in recent years the family got together to re-create it. Rod’s 80-year-old uncle, who painted the original, sprayed the sharp yellow hue on this buggy.


Emory’s Beetles show that not all fun things need to be fancy, fast, or complicated. Sometimes it’s about putting what you have to innovative use and embracing the cool new thing that emerges. Function over form. Or in Emory’s case, function and form. The original Beetle built by the Emory family was featured in magazines of the era, and it seems the desire to take the car further down the coast and south of the border was strong enough to make a nickname stick. Dune buggy or Baja Beetle, we don’t care what you call it, as long as you have fun driving it.
